{{Short description|Cryptographic protocol}}
{{Use dmy dates|date=January 2020}}
In [[cryptography]], '''Combined Elliptic-Curve and Post-Quantum 2''' ('''CECPQ2''') is a [[post-quantum cryptography|quantum-secure]] modification to [[Transport Layer Security]] (TLS) 1.3 developed by [[Google]]. It is intended to be used experimentally, to help evaluate the performance of post-quantum [[key-exchange algorithm]]s on actual users' devices.<ref name="Langley">{{cite web |last1=Langley |first1=Adam |title=CECPQ2 |url=https://www.imperialviolet.org/2018/12/12/cecpq2.html |website=Imperial Violet|date=2018-12-12 |accessdate=5 January 2020}}</ref>

==Details==
Similarly to its predecessor [[CECPQ1]], CECPQ2 aims to provide confidentiality against an attacker with a large scale [[quantum computer]]. It is essentially a plugin for the TLS [[key-agreement protocol|key-agreement]] part. CECPQ2 combines two key exchange mechanisms: the classical [[X25519]] and [[HRSS (cryptography)|HRSS]] (Hülsing, Rijneveld, Schanck, and Schwabe) scheme (an instantiation of the [[NTRU]] [[lattice-based cryptography|lattice based]] [[key exchange]] primitive).<ref name="Langley"/> Additionally, Kris Kwiatkowski has implemented and deployed an alternative version of post-quantum key-exchange algorithm, titled ''CECPQ2b''. Similarly to CECPQ2, this is also a hybrid post-quantum key exchange scheme, that is based on  [[supersingular isogeny key exchange]] (SIKE) instead of HRSS. <ref name="Kwiatkowski">{{cite web |last1=Kwiatkowski |first1=Kris|first2=Luke|last2=Valenta |title=The TLS Post-Quantum Experiment |url=https://blog.cloudflare.com/the-tls-post-quantum-experiment/ |date=2019-10-30|website=Cloudflare Blog |accessdate=31 December 2020}}</ref>

CECPQ2 uses 32 bytes of shared secret material derived from the classical [[X25519]] mechanism, and 32 bytes of shared secret material derived from the quantum-secure HRSS mechanism. The resulting bytes are concatenated and used as secret key. Concatenation is meant to assure that the protocol provides at least the same security level as widely used X25519, should HRSS be found insecure.

The algorithm was to be deployed on both the server side using [[Cloudflare]]'s infrastructure, and the client side using [[Google Chrome]] Canary.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Kwiatkowski |first1=Kris |title=Towards Post-Quantum Cryptography in TLS |url=https://blog.cloudflare.com/towards-post-quantum-cryptography-in-tls/ |website=The Cloudflare Blog |accessdate=5 January 2020  |date=20 June 2019}}</ref> Since both parties need to support the algorithm for it to be chosen, this experiment is available only to Chrome Canary users accessing websites hosted by Cloudflare.

It was estimated that the experiment started mid-2019.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Shankland |first1=Stephen |title=Quantum computers will break today's internet security; Cloudflare wants to fix it |url=https://www.cnet.com/news/quantum-computing-will-break-net-security-cloudflare-wants-to-fix-it/ |publisher=CNET|date=2019-06-20 |accessdate=5 January 2020 }}</ref> It was considered a step in a general program at [[Cloudflare]] to transition to [[post-quantum cryptography|post-quantum safe]] cryptographic primitives.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Kwiatkowski |first1=Kris|last2=Faz-Hernández|first2=Armando |title=Introducing CIRCL: An Advanced Cryptographic Library |url=https://blog.cloudflare.com/introducing-circl/|date=2019-06-20 |accessdate=5 January 2020 |website=Cloudflare Blog}}</ref>

Support for CECPQ2 was removed from [[BoringSSL]] in April 2023.
